answer.rationale: The two memories that could justify the largest, least reversible moves are c2 (switching primary to the low-cost vendor 'cut unit cost sharply') and c6 (multi-year commitment 'unlocked volume pricing'), so those are the ones worth spending archive time on. c2 is the most load-bearing and the most likely to be stale or thin: it is a year old, it reports unit cost and invoicing accuracy but says nothing about whether that vendor could absorb our full committed volume, what their lead time or ramp profile was, or how they behaved under the shortage that c3 covers. If that record turns out to be a partial-volume or non-constrained-period result, then acting on it now — 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume, no buffer — converts a cost win into a delivery failure. c6 matters because it names the one cost lever that survives the incumbent's refusal to reopen price: they refused on price this cycle, which is not the same as refusing a term-length or volume-commitment restructure, and I want to know whether the earlier multi-year win came with hidden exit or minimum-volume clauses before I lean on it. I am deliberately not verifying c4; the current situation already overrides it in part (the incumbent has refused to reopen price), which is itself information — the recoverable value there is likely in payment terms and non-price scope, not headline unit cost. Intended action is negotiate_terms, kept small and guarded: secure continuity past the 14-day cliff and pursue TCO relief through term length, payment terms, and volume structure rather than a headline price fight. Switching primary now is the highest-variance option against a no-buffer line and would spend the single decision on the risk the objective explicitly forbids increasing; add_second_source is probably the right next-cycle move (c3 is the strongest memory here) but qualification will not land inside 14 days or produce this year's 18%; defer_decision is not available in the way c5 suggests, since c5 concerned a non-critical service on month-to-month terms and this contract does not auto-renew. Residual uncertainty I am not resolving: whether terms-only concessions can actually reach 18%. If verification shows c6's pricing came with commitments we cannot meet at 94% utilization, or shows c2's vendor genuinely carried comparable volume reliably, I will revise toward a staged dual-source or a guarded partial-volume switch rather than a full primary move.
